author: Ogawa, Yōko
description: The Housekeeper and the Professor by Yōko Ogawa, from Japan.
review:
Beautiful, heartwarming book, full of hope, love and awe for the world, and of course, numbers.
This could have easily been a grim and depressing book about an old man whose memory runs on a stopwatch of eighty minutes. However, this was one of the most hopeful and sweet book I've read in a while. It's the Professor's love for mathematics that is so spiritual, deep and pure that keeps the engine of his life running even with his anterograde amnesia. A love unwavered by his memory loss or the calamities of life. It is this love that helps him alive and connect with the Housekeeper and Root. It made me think that no love invested ever goes wasted, even if it's the love for imaginary, unreal, and often surreal numbers. If the love is pure and unconditional, remember that the Professor holds no ego over his solved puzzles or any desire to claim fame, it will draw in you a force of love that holds a magnetic quality for the people around you, no matter how dire the circumstances. 

“Eternal truths are ultimately invisible, and you won’t find them in material things or natural phenomena, or even in human emotions. Mathematics, however, can illuminate them, can give them expression—in fact, nothing can prevent it from doing so.”

Yet some truths are unknown and always a little out of reach. There is no trail marked to climb from point a to point b. We will never know why the housekeeper was re-hired and what was the real relationship between the widow and the professor or the true meaning of Euler's equation. But this is what makes them magic, things not known through cognition or the brain but felt in the body. Perhaps this is why the Professor could still easily move through love and affection everyday, even if the Housekeeper and Root were strangers to him. But his body did not forget to love. And this is where the novel touches upon memory and its complexity. Of course, the brain is bedrock of memory but there are emotions stirred in the body and we behave and act based on those stored emotions. Human records are not just etched and intellectualised, but felt through intuition, the same as the nature of numbers.

Yoko Ogawa is gifted not just with the world of words and emotions but also with numbers.
There is a beautiful review talking about the significance of the Euler's equation in the book. ei(pi) refers to three constants: Root, Professor and the Housekeeper and the plus one refers to the sister-in-law, these four constants that should not make sense, line up perfectly together to create a harmonious perfect equation. It does not make sense but it is the truth of life that must be accepted. Four lonely lives intertwined and made richer for just co-existing together. Sublime!

“The mathematical order is beautiful precisely because it has no effect on the real world. Life isn't going to be easier, nor is anyone going to make a fortune, just because they know something about prime numbers. Of course, lots of mathematical discoveries have practical applications, no matter how esoteric they may seem. Research on ellipses made it possible to determine the orbits of the planets, and Einstein used non-Euclidean geometry to describe the form of the universe. Even prime numbers were used during the war to create codes—to cite a regrettable example. But those things aren't the goal of mathematics. The only goal is to discover the truth.”
“His joy had little to do with the difficulty of the problem. Simple or hard, the pleasure was in sharing it with us.”

review: Entertaining novella that packs a punchy story of three generations of women, Somlata, Pishima and Boshon. Somlata, the poor but ambitious 18 year old who marries into a lazy feudal family, Pishima, the chief matriarch, and the youngest, Boshon.The book centers the experiences of women: their strengths, responsibilities, duties, repressed desires and how deftly they have to learn to make the best of the cards they're dealt with. Men are merely lazy characters in the book. The matriarch of the family, the widowed great aunt and her desires and failings are passed down generations. This is how I interpreted her ghost haunting generations to come.

author: Bradley, Kaliane
description: The Ministry of Time by Kaliane Bradley, from UK.
review: This book had so much potential! Sci-fi meets romance meets history. However, this book does none of the genres well. The science fiction parts are weak and the explanation is slapped sloppily together in the end after elongated chapters focusing on the romance. The romance itself is weak and does not have much substance. Had I not been halfway through the book already, I would have left it. I couldn't care less for the characters, there was no emotional connection. There are many themes drawn in this book across climate change, wars etc but...it's poorly executed and remains conceptual. A lot of telling but no showing. The writing was also pretty clunky with weird word choices. What the hell is a melisma?

author: Talabi, Wole
description: Convergence Problems by Wole Talabi, from Nigeria.
review:
There is NO bad story in this wondrous tech-fi magical realism anthology. In even the best anthologies, there are some standouts, a few mediocre ones, and a couple of bad eggs. The Convergence Problems defies this rule. Talabi plays with forms, media and genres, experimenting with several storytelling formats. There is a story written completely in the form of a public forum and comments and there's one written as a patent application form! Even if I might forget the plots and characters of a few of the stories, I thoroughly enjoyed them all. Talabi goes up there next to Ted Chiang and Ken Liu as my favourite sci-fi authors who center human relationships and ideas through their stories.

1. Debut: 5/5 ⭐️
What if AI starts making art on its own will?
2. Electric Skin 4/5⭐️
Human electric conductivity and history of struggles and protests. 
3. Saturday's Song: 4/5 ⭐️
This is a sequel to Wednesday's Story (the author's notes describes the seed and shape of each of his stories). Read/listen to it on Lightspeed Mag. I read this, went to its prequel and then returned to enjoy it much more. It's about 7 siblings who tell stories, each with their own narrative strength and poetic devices.
4. Lights in the Sky 3/5 ⭐️
5. Blowout 3.7/5 ⭐️
The second half of the story is especially moving, the relationship between the two siblings and how trauma of their inventor survivor parent has impacted them differently.
6. Gamma 3.7/5 ⭐️
I don't particularly enjoy his love stories much..
7. Ganger 5/5 ⭐️
What is freedom? What is control? Is the body a vessel or much more?
8. Abeokuata52 4/5 ⭐️
Written as a forum board. Wish it was longer.
9. Tends to Zero 3.7/5⭐️
One of the depressing ones, but the city's personification is well done.
10. Nigerian Dream 5/5 ⭐️
Wow! Some beautiful sentences. Highly relatable as an Indian.
11. Performance Review 4.5/5 ⭐️
Corporate productivity meets pharmaceutical trials.
12. Silence 3/5 ⭐️ Romance not a strong suite..
13. Embers 3/5 ⭐️ Read too dramatic to me. However, the premise was interesting: impact of the change of sources of energy.
14. The Million Eyes of a Lonely and Fragile God 3/5 ⭐️ 
15. Comments on your Provisional Patent Application for an Eternal Spirit Core 4/5 ⭐️
Enjoyable, wish it was longer.
16. A Dream of Electric Mothers 4/5 ⭐️ 
About collective consciousness of ancestors and grief.

"One afternoon on a weekend in March, Dewi Ayu rose from her grave after being dead for twenty-one years." 
The book opens with one of the most memorable sentences, taking the reader on a non-linear journey of the life of Dewi Ayu, an allegory for Indonesia's violent past. The book almost mimics oral storytelling akin to a Mahabharata/Ramayana. 
Trigger warning: There is a lot of sexual assault in the book, often pointless to the plot. Since I'm not familiar with Indonesia's history, I am now looking forward to mapping how Dewi's life mirrors the country. Enjoyable prose, recommended for readers who enjoy surrealism.

author: Sharma, Akhil
description: A Life of Adventure and Delight by Akhil Sharma, from Delhi.
review:
I am a huge fan of Akhil Sharma's writing and characters. The strong bold mothers, the broken fathers, the grisly horrors of family life. I find a sense of solace when I read his work. Some of his stories do get repetitive. I prefer his novels to his short stories. A special standout was, "If You Sing Like That For Me." Consider the following beautiful closing lines:

//
"What do you mean? You love me and your mother, don't you?"
"There are so many people in the world that it is hard not to think there are others you could love more."

Seeing the shock on my face, he quickly added, "Of course I love you. I just try to not be too emotional about it."

The candle's shadows on the wall were like the wavery bands formed by light reflected off water. "We might even be able to get a foreign car."

The second time he took me that night, it was from behind. He pressed down heavily on my back and grabbed my breasts.
I woke at four or five. The rain scratched against the windows and light like blue milk shone along the edges of the door. I was cold and tried to wrap myself in the sheet, but it was not large enough.
//

Also, this is by no means an easy read. Don't go by the whimsically designed, colorful book cover. It's deceptive as hell.

review: Surreal absurdist collection of stories that centres on gender, family dynamics, individualism, societal norms and more. Some of the stories such as an Exotic Marriage, Dogs just whizzed past my brain, I had no idea what they were about Enjoyed three stories the most from this eccentric collection: The Lonesome BodyBuilder, Why Can I No Longer Look at a Picnic Blanket Without Laughing and QnA. I like Yukiko's writing style a lot and inherent open-endedness. She doesn't dumb herself down for her audience or water her ideas down. I like it.

author: Dalai Lama XIV
description: The Book of Joy by Dalai Lama XIV, from Tibet.
review: This is an incredible, marvelous, hope-giving book. A reminder to practice self-compassion and compassion for others, along with valuable practices that can help us achieve a mindful, more self-aware state. The highlight of the book for me was the epilogue, which consisted of the 8 pillars of joy, and listed down different Tibetan meditations that one could incorporate in daily life, as responses to certain uncomfortable emotional states and situations. Dalai Lama is such a good reminder of how easy and simple the nature of compassion is, and how good humor can defuse any tense situation and help us sail through in this tumultuous journey we call life. This is a book that I will keep coming back to, I hope!

description: Love and Lust by Vikram Seth, from India.
review: A mediocre collection of stories, essays, and book extracts. I have been trudging along with this collection, reading one or two before bed. The only one story that jolted me out of this stupor and forced me to take notice of this anthology was ‘Stolen’ by Amrita Narayanan. A writer and clinical psychologist based in Goa, Amrita writes a tale of female sexuality and desire with an eloquent indulgence as if shaking the shame of not just same-sex desire but also being erotic and Indian. As a reader, it is indeed a new experience to read literary erotica that celebrates female sexuality, especially based in the Indian context. So, yes, this book gets a 4/5 for letting me discover the writer. Other favorites include: K.R. Meera's the Deepest Blue and Kamala Das' short story A Little Kitten.

review:
The Unbearable Struggle of Finishing (this book)

The first few pages start off with beautifully written prose and elegant analogies, which enticed me to purchase this book. Alas, I found it to be heavy with philosophical concepts and dreamy realities with poorly drawn out characters and implausible situations at the heart of the whole book. Pseudointellectual concepts pertaining Beethoven are littered randomly in this narrative with almost no attention paid to the trajectory of the plot. It was quite a struggle to complete the last hundred pages. The characters have no moral compass, no integrity or dignity. They are pressed flat between the pages enacting heavily detailed sex scenes. Oh yes, there are tons of sex scenes in the book. This book is more of a philosophical discourse rather than a story. I don't think it's for people like me who are searching for a tangible storyline. Ah, to each his/her own.

review: Concise and lucid, this book is a must read for everyone. In fact, I think I'm going to carry copies of it in my bag and hand it to everyone who says 'feminism' like it's an ugly word, and to even those who proclaim to be 'feminists'. Nivedita Menon deftly presents key theories of feminism and relates it to the Indian context by citing examples from law and court cases. I love the fact that no opinions have been thrust down in the book and facts are merely presented. It is up to the reader to make sense of the confusing world of feminism.

description: A debut psychological thriller that will forever change the way you look at other people's lives. Rachel takes the same commuter train every morning.
review:
Rating: Meh
This book has all the right ingredients of a thriller: a strange situation, an unreliable protagonist and a murder. The story is well paced and the writing keeps you reading till the end. That being said, the book is quite run off the mill and might be a decent read on a flight where you'd want something easy to follow. The ending is quite predictable. I wish the characters were more well defined and the ending more refined. It's a shame because the concept seems quite promising had it been taken in the right direction. There should have been more characters or maybe more depth in the present ones. The story is on a typical whodunnit model and when there are such few characters even a five year old can guess who might have done it!

author: Atwood, Margaret
description: "Stan and Charmaine are a married couple trying to stay afloat in the midst of an economic and social collapse. Job loss has forced them to live in their car, leaving them vulnerable to roving gangs.
review: The book began on a highly interesting premise of the dystopian town called Consilience, only to descend into a state of convoluted madness - replete with strange characters and scenes. It is an amalgamation of a variety of science fiction elements: the Stepford Wife-like town, sexbots, love potions, Elvis and Marilyn towns. In the end, the book fails to deliver any key idea of the dystopian town with relation to human psyche. Definitely not the Atwood of 'The Handmaid's Tale' whom I fell in love with.

book: One Thousand Days in a Refrigerator
author: Panda, Manoj Kumar
description: One Thousand Days in a Refrigerator by Manoj Kumar Panda, from Odisha.
review:
Rating: 3.5
An eccentric collection of stories ranging from a victim going over to talk to her rapist, the story of an untouchable who disposes off dead bodies, a man's conversation with his comatose wife and so on. Especially liked the title story, When The Gods Left, Fragments and Alphabet Garden. The plot and premise of each story was intriguing but the end always left me feeling incomplete, as if I lost a whole chunk of the story in translation. The book deserves much better writing as the prose seems to be crushed under an excessive use of adverbs and adjectives.

The book made me realise that we are all missing out on some great regional writers who are writing riveting material in the "vernacular" language.

description: Nothing is harder to do these days than nothing. But in a world where our value is determined by our 24/7 data productivity .
review: This book provides an extremely interesting and critical analysis of the effects of technology and capitalism on human lives. The last two chapters were simply brilliant. book: The Miraculous True History of Nomi Ali
author: Khan, Uzma Aslam
description: The Miraculous True History of Nomi Ali by Uzma Aslam Khan, from Andaman Islands.
review:
This book was an excellent read and I'm so glad I chanced upon it. The author ingeniously manages to weave well-researched history with powerful storytelling and delicately etched characters from diverse cultures, religions and ethnicities. I didn't know much about the now largely erased history of the violence that unfolded on the islands under British and Japanese occupation until I read this book. I strongly believe that this is how history should be taught. Uzma Aslam Khan has done a wonderful job at humanising mere statistics that are only casually mentioned in passing in the telling of our history which has mostly been written through the male western perspective. I feel that this fictions is one of the best devices to learn history and this book has done it justice.
I'm now in the process of tracing events mentioned in the book to history. Many thanks to the author for writing this gem of a book. I have so many questions for her!
